bicycle.line: A bicycle is just a metal spider with two round feet that cannot climb rocks.
facts: Bicycles use human pedaling power to turn wheels and move forward along the ground.
The first bicycle was invented over two hundred years ago without any pedals at all.

car.line: A car. Fast. Cannot climb stairs.
facts: Cars usually have four wheels and an engine that burns fuel to make them drive.
Most cars carry seats for several people to sit inside while traveling on roads.

motorcycle.line: A motorcycle is a loud metal beetle that balances on two wheels instead of four.
facts: Motorcycles only have two wheels, so riders must wear helmets to stay safe.
Riders lean into a turn so the motorcycle keeps its balance.

airplane.line: An airplane is a giant silver bird that lacks feathers and lands on flat concrete.
facts: Airplanes use big wings and powerful engines to fly high up in the sky.
They need long runways on the ground to take off and land safely.

bus.line: A bus is a very long yellow caterpillar that carries too many people at once.
facts: Buses are large vehicles designed to transport many passengers along city streets.
They follow specific routes and stop at designated places to let people on and off.

train.line: A train is a stubborn metal centipede that refuses to leave its iron tracks.
facts: Trains run on steel tracks and are made of multiple connected cars pulling together.
They can carry heavy cargo and hundreds of passengers across long distances.

truck.line: A truck is a heavy pack animal made of steel that carries boxes instead of grass.
facts: Trucks are built strong and sturdy to haul heavy loads and big supplies.
Some trucks are massive semi-trailers that transport goods from city to city.

boat.line: A boat is a wooden floating hoof that sinks instantly if the water turns to air.
facts: Boats float on top of water because their hulls push water out of the way.
People use oars, sails, or motors to steer boats across lakes, rivers, and oceans.

traffic light.line: A traffic light is a bossy glowing totem pole that tells metal boxes when to stop.
facts: Traffic lights use red, yellow, and green lights to keep cars and pedestrians safe.
Red means stop, green means go, and yellow means slow down before stopping.

fire hydrant.line: A fire hydrant is a short iron stump that keeps a cold drink ready for big red trucks.
facts: Fire hydrants connect to underground pipes full of water to help put out fires.
Firefighters attach long hoses to them to get enough water during emergencies.

stop sign.line: A stop sign is a red octagon that yells at metal boxes to freeze in their tracks.
facts: Stop signs always have eight sides and are painted bright red with white letters.
Drivers must bring their vehicles to a complete halt before driving past them.

parking meter.line: A parking meter is a greedy metal clock that demands shiny coins to sit on asphalt.
facts: Parking meters let drivers pay for a specific amount of time to leave a car parked.
When the time runs out, a small flag pops up or the screen turns red.

bench.line: A bench is a flat wooden shelf where tired flat-landers sit down to stare at nothing.
facts: Benches are outdoor seats usually found in parks, gardens, and along city sidewalks.
They are built long enough for multiple people to sit and rest at the same time.

bird.line: A bird is a tiny flying rival that thinks it owns the air above my favorite peak.
facts: Birds have feathers, wings, and lightweight bones that help them fly through the air.
Most birds hatch from hard-shelled eggs built in nests high up off the ground.

cat.line: A cat is a soft little rock-hopper who sleeps all day and refuses to carry gear.
facts: Cats have whiskers and sharp claws that help them balance and climb very well.
They communicate their moods by purring, meowing, and twitching their tails.

dog.line: A dog lacks the proper hoof-action for genuine ridgeline exploration.
facts: Dogs can smell things tens of thousands of times better than humans can.
Most dogs have wet noses to help them capture scent chemicals in the air.

horse.line: A horse. Tall, fast, and hopeless on a ledge.
facts: Horses are able to sleep while standing up on their long legs.
A horse has the largest eyes of any land mammal on earth.

sheep.line: A sheep has respectable wool but gives up entirely too easily on steep inclines.
facts: Sheep have rectangular pupils that let them see almost all around themselves.
A group of sheep is commonly known as a flock.

cow.line: A cow belongs strictly in the valley where the ground remains flat and boring.
facts: Cows spend up to a third of every day eating grass and other plants.
A cow has four compartments in its stomach to help digest tough food.

elephant.line: An elephant brings far too much bulk to any respectable mountain ledge.
facts: Elephants are the largest land animals alive on earth today.
An elephant uses its long trunk to breathe and drink water.

bear.line: A bear insists on sleeping through the best months of the climbing calendar.
facts: Bears spend the winter months resting in dens to save energy.
Many bears are excellent climbers despite their heavy build.

zebra.line: A zebra wears striking stripes but completely misses the point of elevation.
facts: Every zebra has a unique pattern of black and white stripes.
Zebras live together in family groups called harems.

giraffe.line: A giraffe reaches impressive heights yet avoids all actual rock faces.
facts: Giraffes are the tallest mammals living on the planet.
A giraffe has a long dark tongue used to reach high leaves.

backpack.line: A backpack carries useful gear instead of useful opinions about the trail.
facts: Backpacks help spread heavy loads evenly across your shoulders and back.
Early backpack frames were often made of wood or wicker.

umbrella.line: An umbrella is a nervous little roof that panics at the first sign of weather.
facts: Umbrellas were originally invented to shade people from the sun.
Modern umbrellas often use lightweight metal frames and waterproof fabric.

handbag.line: A handbag stores tiny human treasures instead of proper trail snacks.
facts: Handbags became very common for carrying personal items in daily life.
Small bags have been used by humans for hundreds of years.

tie.line: A tie hangs uselessly about like a strip of cloth with no real purpose.
facts: Neckties are worn around the collar as a decorative clothing accessory.
Modern ties are usually knotted and worn with collared shirts.

suitcase.line: A suitcase stays firmly on flat pavement and avoids all rugged terrain.
facts: Suitcases are designed with handles to make traveling easier.
Some modern suitcases have small wheels attached to the bottom.

frisbee.line: A frisbee sails through the air when thrown but lacks any climbing ambition.
facts: Flying discs were originally inspired by pie tins tossed in the air.
The aerodynamic shape helps the disc glide smoothly across open spaces.

skis.line: Skis slide foolishly down the slope instead of climbing sensibly upward.
facts: Skis attach to boots to help people glide across snow surfaces.
Ancient skis were used for winter travel long before modern sports.

snowboard.line: A snowboard is just a heavy leaf for sliding down slopes where moss belongs.
facts: People strap both feet to this board to slide down snowy mountain slopes fast.
Snowboarding became an official winter sport in the Olympics years ago.

sports ball.line: An ordinary sports ball rolls away when you drop it on a proper ledge.
facts: Balls are usually round so they can roll smoothly across the ground in games.
Different sports use different kinds of balls made of rubber, leather, or plastic.

kite.line: A kite. A thing that climbs with no legs. Suspicious.
facts: Kites use the wind blowing through the sky to stay up high in the air.
People hold onto a long string attached to the kite to keep it from flying away.

baseball bat.line: A baseball bat looks like a heavy tree branch stripped of all its good bark.
facts: Players use this wooden or metal club to hit a pitched ball during a game.
Batters wear a helmet to keep their heads safe while holding the bat.

baseball glove.line: An oversized leather hand like this baseball glove has no business on a hoof.
facts: Fielders wear this large leather mitt on their hand to catch flying balls safely.
The webbing between the fingers helps players trap the ball in the pocket.

skateboard.line: A skateboard is a tiny wooden deck with four wheels that hate loose gravel.
facts: Skaters stand on the board and push with one foot to roll along flat pavement.
The bottom of the board often has colorful pictures printed on the flat surface.

surfboard.line: A surfboard is a giant flat leaf meant for riding angry ocean waves instead of rocks.
facts: Surfers lie or stand on this long board to ride ocean waves toward the shore.
Wax is rubbed on the top surface so feet do not slip off while riding.

tennis racket.line: A tennis racket is a weird net frame meant for swatting fuzzy green spheres.
facts: Players use the strung oval head of the racket to hit a fuzzy ball over a net.
The handle is wrapped in tape so players can keep a firm grip during the match.

bottle.line: An empty bottle makes a hollow clink when it rolls down a rocky gully.
facts: Bottles have narrow necks designed to hold liquids without spilling them out.
Many plastic and glass bottles can be recycled to make brand new items.

wine glass.line: A wine glass is a terribly fragile goblet that would shatter on my first leap.
facts: This delicate glass stands on a thin stem so hands do not warm the drink.
It has a wide bowl at the top to let the liquid breathe and release aromas.

cup.line: A cup is just a miniature watering trough with a handle for clumsy fingers.
facts: Cups have open tops and are used for holding drinks like water or milk.
Most cups have a small handle on the side so fingers stay away from hot liquids.

fork.line: A fork is a tiny metal rake for scraping up bits of stray vegetation.
facts: A fork has several narrow metal prongs at the end for piercing food pieces.
People use forks to lift food to their mouths without using their fingers.

knife.line: A sharp knife is a thin sliver of metal that lacks the grace of a good horn.
facts: Knives have a sharp metal blade used for cutting and slicing various items.
The handle is designed for a person to hold safely while using the blade.

spoon.line: A spoon is a shallow metal scoop that is utterly useless for climbing.
facts: A spoon has a small round bowl shape at the end for holding liquids or soft food.
People use spoons to eat soup, cereal, and other foods that would slide off a fork.

bowl.line: A bowl is a round stone basin carved by humans instead of rushing water.
facts: Bowls are round and deep, making them great for holding foods like cereal or soup.
The curved sides keep liquid and loose food from spilling over the edges.

banana.line: A banana. Comes with its own wrapper. Respect.
facts: Bananas grow hanging upside down from tall plants that look like trees but are really giant herbs.
A bunch of bananas is technically called a hand, and the single ones are called fingers.

apple.line: An apple sits there looking round and smug because it has never fallen down a scree slope.
facts: Apples float in water because twenty five percent of their volume is actually made of air.
Apple trees first grew wild in the mountains of Central Asia, and some wild ones still grow there.

sandwich.line: A sandwich is just two slices of bread guarding something that lacks the courage to stand alone.
facts: The sandwich was named after an English nobleman who wanted to eat meat without leaving the card table.
Sliced bread was first sold in stores using a machine invented by Otto Frederick Rohwedder.

orange.line: An orange rolls too easily to be trusted on any incline steeper than a gentle meadow.
facts: Oranges are a hybrid of pomelos and mandarins, which means they are not an original wild fruit.
Brazil is the country that grows the most oranges in the entire world.

broccoli.line: A broccoli looks like a tiny green pine tree that grew sideways and lost its ambition.
facts: Broccoli belongs to the same family of plants as cabbage and kale.
The word broccoli comes from an Italian plural word meaning the flowering crest of a cabbage.

carrot.line: A carrot points straight down into the dirt instead of reaching upward toward the peaks.
facts: Wild carrots used to be purple or yellow before farmers bred them to be orange.
The orange part of a carrot is its root, where the plant stores food underground.

hot dog.line: A hot dog is hiding inside a soft roll because it knows it cannot survive the open air.
facts: Frankfurters or hot dogs originated in Germany, taking their name from a famous city there.
People in the United States eat billions of hot dogs every single year during summer holidays.

pizza.line: A pizza is flat and round, two traits I find deeply suspicious in any object whatsoever.
facts: Modern pizza was invented in the city of Naples in Italy as a quick meal for workers.
Pizza with tomato sauce came after tomatoes reached Europe from the Americas.

donut.line: A donut has a hole in the middle because it lacks the solid center of a proper boulder.
facts: Some bakers put holes in donuts so the center would cook evenly without staying raw.
Donuts were originally called olykoeks, which translates to oily cakes in Dutch.

cake.line: A cake is far too soft to withstand even a mild gust of wind above the timberline.
facts: Ancient cakes were much more like bread and were sweetened with honey and dried fruit.
The ancient Greeks made round honey cakes and lit candles on them to glow like the moon.

chair.line: A chair stays rigidly in one spot instead of seeking out the highest vantage point.
facts: Chairs used to be rare luxury items used only by important leaders and wealthy people.
Ancient Egyptians made some of the earliest known chairs out of ebony and ivory.

couch.line: A couch invites you to lie completely flat, which is a terrible way to admire the scenery.
facts: Couches evolved from long benches that had cushions placed on them for extra comfort.
The word sofa comes from an Arabic word meaning a bench decorated with cushions.

potted plant.line: A potted plant is a mountain shrub that got scared and trapped itself inside pottery.
facts: Plants grown in pots need holes in the bottom so their roots do not drown in water.
Indoor plants help clean the air inside buildings by absorbing certain gases through leaves.

bed.line: A bed is just a horizontal platform for wasting daylight hours that could be spent climbing.
facts: Ancient Egyptians slept on raised wooden frames to keep away from scorpions and snakes.
Humans spend about one third of their entire lives sleeping in a bed.

dining table.line: A dining table is a flat wooden plateau completely devoid of interesting rocks or moss.
facts: The ancient Romans used to recline on couches around their low dining tables to eat meals.
Rectangular dining tables became popular in medieval Europe in large castle halls.

toilet.line: A toilet is just an indoor puddle with too much ambition.
facts: Toilets use a lot of clean water every single time they flush.
Indoor plumbing helps keep cities clean and healthy.

tv.line: A television is a window showing flat moving pictures of places without rocks.
facts: Televisions use lots of tiny colored dots called pixels to make pictures.
The very first televisions only showed images in black and white.

laptop.line: A laptop is a metal clam that glows instead of making pearls.
facts: Laptops have rechargeable batteries so you can use them without plugging them in.
The keyboard and screen are built into one folding piece.

mouse.line: A computer mouse is a plastic rodent that stays in one spot.
facts: A computer mouse helps you point at things on the screen.
Older mice used a rolling rubber ball underneath to track movement.

remote.line: A remote control is a magic wand for people who hate walking across rooms.
facts: Remote controls usually use invisible light beams to talk to the TV.
They are one of the most commonly lost items in a house.

keyboard.line: A keyboard. A hundred buttons and not one for climbing.
facts: Most computer keyboards arrange their top letters in a pattern called QWERTY.
The longest word you can type using only the top row of letters is typewriter.

cell phone.line: A cell phone is a tiny glass brick that whispers secrets from far away.
facts: Cell phones use invisible radio waves to send calls and messages through the air.
Modern phones are tiny computers that can fit right in your pocket.

microwave.line: A microwave is a small metal box that makes cold food hot in seconds.
facts: Microwaves cook food by making water molecules inside it vibrate very fast.
They were invented by accident when a radar scientist melted a candy bar.

oven.line: An oven is a warm indoor cave used for baking flat things.
facts: Ovens use high heat to cook food all the way through from the outside in.
They can get much hotter than a normal room ever gets.

toaster.line: A toaster is a metal box that turns soft bread into crunchy slices.
facts: Toasters use glowing hot wires to toast bread very quickly.
Springs inside push the toast back up when it is finished.

sink.line: A sink is a stone basin where water appears and disappears on command.
facts: Sinks have a curved pipe underneath called a trap to catch heavy dirt.
Running water in sinks helps people wash their hands to stay healthy.

refrigerator.line: A refrigerator is a giant metal cupboard that stays cold inside.
facts: Refrigerators use special liquids and pumps to push heat out of the box.
Keeping food cold slows down germs and helps it stay fresh longer.

book.line: A book is a stack of dead tree leaves covered in tiny ink tracks.
facts: Books let you explore imaginary worlds without leaving your chair.
The spine holds all the paper pages together so they do not fall out.

clock.line: A clock is a round metal face that worries about the time constantly.
facts: Clocks use numbers from one to twelve to show the hours of the day.
The short hand points to the hour and the long hand points to the minute.

vase.line: A vase is a hollow stone pot meant to hold headless plants.
facts: Vases are usually made of glass, clay, or ceramic materials.
They hold water to keep cut flowers looking fresh for a few days.

scissors.line: An absurd metal beak designed for people who cannot bite their own wool.
facts: Scissors use two blades that slide past each other to slice things cleanly.
The oldest known scissors date back thousands of years to ancient Egypt.

teddy bear.line: A stuffed imitation of a predator that lacks the decency to stand on rocks.
facts: Teddy bears were named after President Theodore Roosevelt after he refused to shoot a bear.
Early teddy bears were stuffed with wood shavings instead of soft fluff.

hair drier.line: A howling wind machine that completely fails to dry damp mountain fog.
facts: Hair dryers use a fan and a heating element to speed up the evaporation of water.
The first home hair dryers were heavy and blew air through a metal hose.

toothbrush.line: A tiny plastic pine tree meant for scraping the moss off your grinding stones.
facts: Toothbrushes help remove food bits and plaque from teeth to keep them strong.
Ancient people used twigs with frayed ends to clean their teeth long ago.

tree.line: A giant wooden ladder that refuses to let goats use its top rungs.
facts: Trees make their own food using sunlight through a process called photosynthesis.
The rings inside a tree trunk can show how many years the tree has lived.

flower.line: A brightly colored snack signal that only bees are allowed to appreciate.
facts: Flowers contain seeds or pollen to help new plants grow in the soil.
Bright colors and sweet smells attract insects and birds to visit flowers.

trash can.line: A smelly metal cave where humans hide all their discarded treasures.
facts: Trash cans keep public areas clean by holding items people no longer need.
Many items placed in bins today are sorted out to be recycled into new things.

street lamp.line: A tall metal sun that stays awake long after the real sky goes to sleep.
facts: Street lamps light up dark roads to help people walk safely at night.
Modern street lamps often use energy efficient bulbs to save power.

squirrel.line: A jittery fuzzball that treats every vertical surface like a personal race.
facts: Squirrels bury nuts in the ground and sometimes forget where they put them.
A squirrel uses its bushy tail for balance when it leaps through the trees.

duck.line: A duck. Floats, flies and walks. A show-off, honestly.
facts: Ducks have waterproof feathers that keep them dry when they swim.
Webbed feet help ducks paddle smoothly across the surface of the water.

goose.line: An aggressive grey feather bag with a very high opinion of itself.
facts: Geese fly together in a large V shape when they migrate for the winter.
Geese are very loud and will hiss loudly to protect their territory.

rabbit.line: A twitchy ground jumper that has never attempted a proper mountain ridge.
facts: Rabbits live in underground burrows to stay safe from larger animals.

deer.line: A tall gangly jumper that slips on scree because it lacks proper hooves.
facts: Male deer grow antlers on their heads that fall off and grow back each year.

butterfly.line: A confused leaf scrap that flutters around without any sense of direction.
facts: Butterflies start their lives as crawling caterpillars before changing shape.

mushroom.line: A suspicious rubbery umbrella sprouting straight out of the damp dirt.
facts: Mushrooms are neither plants nor animals but belong to the fungus kingdom.
Many mushrooms grow very fast overnight after a good rain shower.
